questions.question: What is the difference between a pseudo-class and a pseudo-element?
questions.title: Pseudo-classes versus pseudo-elements
questions.direct_answer: A pseudo-class selects an existing element when it has a state or structural relationship, such as :focus-visible or :first-child. A pseudo-element represents a part or abstraction not directly represented by an element in the source tree, such as ::first-line or ::before.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can distinguish selecting an element's condition from styling a represented subpart.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling ::before a real child element or treating :hover as a separate piece of content.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use state, structure, and generated-content examples with the correct syntax.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Pseudo-classes select elements by state or relationship.
Pseudo-elements represent a subpart or CSS-created abstraction.
Pseudo-classes normally use one colon; pseudo-elements use two.
Neither syntax inserts a normal DOM element.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A pseudo-class adds a condition to a selector for an element that already exists. `button:focus-visible` matches a button while it needs a visible focus indicator, and `li:first-child` matches an `li` based on its position among siblings.

A pseudo-element represents something below the element level that is not a normal source element. `p::first-line` selects the rendered first line, whose text can change as the layout changes, while `button::before` creates a generated box before the button's actual contents.

For example, `.field:invalid` can style an existing input whose value fails constraint validation. `.field::placeholder` instead targets the placeholder representation inside that input. The first is a state; the second is a represented part.

Modern syntax uses a single colon for pseudo-classes and a double colon for pseudo-elements. Browsers still accept single-colon spelling for some older pseudo-elements, but double colon makes the distinction clear. Pseudo-elements do not become ordinary DOM nodes that JavaScript can query independently.

I use pseudo-classes to express a meaningful selector condition and pseudo-elements for optional visual treatment of a subpart. Essential content and interactive controls remain in HTML, where they have reliable semantics, focus behaviour, and accessibility.

sections.title: Condition versus represented part
sections.content: Ask what the selector is pointing at. If it matches an existing element under a condition, it is a pseudo-class. If it represents a line, marker, placeholder, or generated before/after box, it is a pseudo-element attached to an originating element.

sections.title: Both extend selection without rewriting the source tree
sections.content: A structural pseudo-class such as `:nth-child()` evaluates relationships already present in the document tree. A pseudo-element creates a selector target based on layout or CSS concepts that the tree does not directly expose. Because `::first-line` depends on wrapping, resizing can change which characters it represents. Because `::before` is generated presentation, important wording placed there may be absent or inconsistent in accessibility and copying workflows.

sections.title: What each selector represents
sections.content:
| Selector | Matches or represents | Kind |
|---|---|---|
| button:disabled | Existing disabled button | Pseudo-class |
| li:first-child | Existing li in a relationship | Pseudo-class |
| p::first-line | Rendered first line | Pseudo-element |
| li::marker | List marker box | Pseudo-element |

sections.title: Style a state and a subpart separately
sections.content:
```html
<style>
  input:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #d97706; outline-offset: 2px; }
  input::placeholder { color: #667085; }
</style>
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email" placeholder="name@example.com">
```
:focus-visible selects the input in a state; ::placeholder styles one represented part of it.

questions.question: What is the difference between :nth-child() and :nth-of-type()?
questions.title: :nth-child() versus :nth-of-type()
questions.direct_answer: :nth-child() tests an element's position among all element siblings, while :nth-of-type() tests its position among siblings with the same element name. The two differ as soon as other element types appear between the target siblings.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can evaluate structural selectors against actual sibling order.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reading article:nth-child(2) as the second article rather than an article that is the second child.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Trace a mixed sibling list and mention selector fragility when markup changes.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: :nth-of-type() counts siblings with the same element name.
The element must still match the selector before the pseudo-class.
Mixed markup exposes the difference between the two.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`:nth-child()` evaluates the target's position in the full list of element siblings. `article:nth-child(2)` therefore means an article that is also the second element child of its parent; it does not simply mean the second article.

`:nth-of-type()` filters the count by element name. `article:nth-of-type(2)` matches the second article among its siblings even if a heading, paragraph, or another element type appears before or between the articles.

For example, in a section containing `h2, article, aside, article`, the first article is child two and article-of-type one. The second article is child four and article-of-type two. `article:nth-child(2)` selects the first, while `article:nth-of-type(2)` selects the second.

Both selectors describe document structure, so inserting wrapper or decorative elements can change their result. If the design cares about a stable business category rather than sibling position, a class or data attribute usually communicates that intent better.

I choose `nth-child` when the complete sibling sequence matters and `nth-of-type` when the position among one element name matters. I test with realistic mixed markup, because an all-article demo makes the selectors look identical.

sections.title: Count the right sibling set
sections.content: The formula inside both functions selects positions such as odd, 2n, or 3n+1. What changes is the list being counted: every element child for :nth-child(), or only siblings of the same element type for :nth-of-type().

sections.title: A selector before :nth-child() does not filter the count
sections.content: In `.card:nth-child(2)`, the browser first asks whether an element is a `.card` and then whether its position among all element siblings is two. The `.card` selector does not create a card-only counting list. Selectors Level 4 also allows `:nth-child(2 of .card)` to count a filtered selector list, but plain `:nth-child(2)` retains the all-sibling meaning. Clear classes remain preferable when order has no semantic importance.

sections.title: One parent with mixed children
sections.content:
position:       1       2          3       4
child:        h2   article #1    aside   article #2
nth-child:          matches 2             matches 4
nth-of-type:        article 1             article 2

sections.title: See the difference in mixed markup
sections.content:
```html

Updates

First article; second child
Tip
Second article; fourth child
``` The border reaches the first article; the background reaches the second article.

questions.question: When should you use ::before and ::after generated content?
questions.title: Using ::before and ::after responsibly
questions.direct_answer: Use ::before and ::after for decorative or supplementary presentation attached to an existing element, such as a badge shape or quotation mark. Put essential wording and controls in HTML because generated content is not a dependable source for semantics, selection, translation, or accessibility.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner separates decorative CSS content from meaningful document content.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Placing required labels, status messages, or interactive controls in the content property.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the generated boxes, positioning context, and accessibility boundary.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: ::before and ::after generate boxes attached to an originating element.
The content property is required for ordinary generated text or symbols.
Decorative generated content should not carry essential meaning.
Pseudo-elements cannot replace semantic HTML or focusable controls.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`::before` and `::after` create generated pseudo-element boxes before or after an element's real contents. CSS can style and position those boxes, which makes them useful for decorative marks, overlays, shapes, or a visual cue whose meaning is already expressed in HTML.

For example, a link whose visible text already says 'External documentation' can receive a small arrow made with `::after`. If the arrow fails to render, the link still has its name and remains fully usable.

Essential content should not exist only in the `content` property. CSS-generated text may behave inconsistently in accessibility trees, can be missed by translation and search workflows, and is awkward to select or copy. A validation error, price, button label, or status therefore belongs in the document.

Pseudo-elements also are not normal child nodes. JavaScript cannot select `element::before` as an independent DOM object, and a pseudo-element cannot become a genuine focusable button. Its containing element supplies the positioning and interaction context.

I use generated content as progressive visual enhancement: remove the stylesheet and the page should retain the same information and controls. That test keeps CSS responsible for presentation while HTML carries the product's meaning.

sections.title: A generated box is presentation attached to an element
sections.content: The originating element remains the DOM object. The pseudo-element gives CSS an extra stylable box in that element's formatting structure. It can support the message, but it should not be the only place where the message exists.

sections.title: Decoration and information need different failure rules
sections.content: A decorative dot can disappear without changing what a user can understand or do. A required-field marker is more subtle: the asterisk may be decorative only if the label or instructions already state that the field is required and the input has the correct required semantics. When generated content repeats existing meaning, hide or simplify it for assistive technology where appropriate rather than assuming all user agents expose it identically.

sections.title: Decide where the content belongs
sections.content:
Does losing this content change meaning or a task?
├─ yes → real HTML + suitable semantics
└─ no  → ::before / ::after can provide decoration
          ↓
      page still works with CSS removed

sections.title: Add a decorative cue to a complete link
sections.content: ```html CSS specifications ``` The link text remains descriptive without the arrow, so the pseudo-element is only enhancement.

questions.question: How do :is(), :where(), and :not() affect matching and specificity?
questions.title: :is(), :where(), and :not()
questions.direct_answer: :is() matches an element when one selector in its list matches, :not() matches when none match, and :where() matches like :is() but always contributes zero specificity. :is() and :not() take the specificity of their most specific relevant argument rather than adding their own pseudo-class weight.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can simplify selector lists without accidentally raising specificity.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Counting :is() or :not() as one ordinary pseudo-class, or assuming :where() has the argument's weight.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use :where() for override-friendly defaults and trace one exact specificity tuple.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: :not() rejects elements matched by its selector list.
:where() matches like :is() but contributes zero specificity.
:is(), :not(), and :has() use the most specific argument's weight.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`:is()` groups alternatives at one point in a selector. `:is(header, main, footer) a` matches links in any of those regions. `:not()` expresses the opposite condition, such as `button:not(:disabled)`, while `:where()` has the same matches-any behaviour as `:is()`.

Their specificity is intentionally special. `:is()`, `:not()`, and `:has()` do not add a normal pseudo-class point; the most specific selector in their argument list supplies their weight. `:where()` and all of its arguments contribute zero.

For example, `.card :is(h2, #featured)` has ID-level specificity because `#featured` is in the list, even when the element currently matched is an `h2`. Replacing `:is` with `:where` leaves only `.card` contributing, so later component rules are easier to override.

These functions improve readability, but a powerful argument can quietly make a reusable selector difficult to override. I avoid mixing IDs into a broad `:is()` list unless that strength is deliberate, and I use `:where()` for library defaults whose consumers should control presentation.

The choice is therefore both semantic and architectural: use `:is` when grouped alternatives should keep their weight, `:where` when they should not add weight, and `:not` for a clear exclusion condition.

sections.title: Matching logic and selector weight are separate decisions
sections.content: All three functions decide whether a selector matches. Only :where() deliberately erases the weight of its argument list. This lets a stylesheet express a detailed structural filter without forcing consumers to write an even stronger selector later.

sections.title: One strong alternative can strengthen the whole list
sections.content: For specificity calculation, `:is(.note, #urgent)` adopts the ID tuple because it is the most specific argument. That surprises developers who only expect the currently obvious class branch to matter. Keeping strong selectors out of shared lists prevents accidental escalation. In contrast, `:where(article, aside) > :where(h2, h3)` has zero specificity until another selector outside the :where() functions contributes weight.

sections.title: Matching and specificity rules
sections.content:
| Function | Match condition | Specificity contribution |
|---|---|---|
| :is(list) | Any argument matches | Most specific argument |
| :not(list) | No argument matches | Most specific argument |
| :where(list) | Any argument matches | Always 0-0-0 |
